Session 1 reminder: Point forecasts and Forecast Distribution

\(y_t\) random variable to be forecast. Subscript \(t\) indicates observation at time \(t\)

Prediction interval or interval forecast: a range of values of \(y_t\) with a given probability to occur.

Let us see an example with the data below (trend of international arrivals to Australia. Seasonality has been removed):

Let us now focus only on the forecasting region. The figure below depicts the forecast with 80% and 95% at the top and the corresponding forecast distributions for each year below. Note that there are only forecasts at the specific quarters (discrete, quarterly data).

Recall from the session on benchmark models that the point forecast is the mean of the forecast distribution.

Forecast distributions

Most time series models produce normally distributed forecasts.

Prediction intervals

  • Interval within which we expect \(y_t\) to lie with a specified probability.
  • Assuming a normal forecast distribution we may build a two-sided confidence interval for our forecast as follows:

\[ \hat{y}_{T+h|T} \pm c \hat\sigma_h, \]

where:

  • \(\hat\sigma_h\) is an estimate of the standard deviation of the \(h\)-step forecast distribution.
  • the multiplier \(c\) depends on the coverage probability and is equal to the corresponding quantile of the standard normal distribution \(N(0,1)\). Usually we will compute 80% and 95% intervals, although another coverage may be used.
std. normal quantiles
alpha percentage coefficient `c`
0.50 0.50 0.67
0.45 0.55 0.76
0.40 0.60 0.84
0.35 0.65 0.93
0.30 0.70 1.04
0.25 0.75 1.15
0.20 0.80 1.28
0.15 0.85 1.44
0.10 0.90 1.64
0.05 0.95 1.96
0.04 0.96 2.05
0.03 0.97 2.17
0.02 0.98 2.33
0.01 0.99 2.58

Intervals for one-step forecasts

When forecasting one step ahead (h=1), the standard deviation of the forecast distribution can be estimated using the standard deviation of the residuals. The reason for this is that residuals are, after all, one step ahead forecasts. So we may use them to estimate \(\sigma_1\) (sigma for h=1)

\[ \hat{\sigma_1} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T-K}\sum_{t=1}^T e_t^2} \]

  • \(T\) is the length of the residuals (after removing NAs).
  • \(K\) is the number of parameters of the particular model being fitted.

Intervals for multi-step forecasts

Prediction intervals usually increase in width as the forecast horizon increases. The further ahead we forecast, the more uncertainty associated with the forecast, resulting in wider prediction intervals.

Explicit formulas for multi-step forecasts variance

For some methods (e.g. the benchmark methods), it is possible to derive explicit mathematical expressions for the multi-step forecast variance. The derivation of these formulas will is not part of this introductory subject. However it is not always the case that the forecast method of choice has such simple explicit formulas for the forecast variance. Below some examples:

Benchmark method h-step forecast standard deviation
Mean \(\hat{\sigma_1}_h=\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{1+1/T}\)
Naïve \(\hat{\sigma_1}_h=\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h}\)
Seasonal naïve \(\hat{\sigma_1}_h=\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{k+1}\)
Drift \(\hat{\sigma_1}_h=\hat{\sigma}\sqrt{h(1+h/T)}\)
  • \(T\) is the length of the residuals (after removing NAs).
  • \(h\) - the forecast horizon
  • \(\hat\sigma_1\) - standard deviation of the residuals.
  • \(k\) - k is the integer part of \((h-1)/m\), where \(m\) is the seasonal period.
    • in other words, \(k\) is the number of complete seasonal periods in the forecast prior to time \(T+h\)

For other models, the formulas become more complex.

More general approach - Bootstrap residuals

The prediction intervals returned by the fable() package we are using can be relied upon as long as we fulfil the corresponding normality and homoskedasticity of the residuals.

When this is not the case, we may resort to bootstrapping to obtain the multi-step forecast variances of a given method. This assumes uncorrelated residuals with constant variance (homoskedastic residuals), but makes no assumption about normality.

Computing prediction intervals with the fable() package

Let us go through a practical example to illustrate how we can handle the prediction intervals returned by fable()

google_stock <- gafa_stock %>%
  filter(Symbol == "GOOG", year(Date) >= 2015) %>%
  
  # Create regularly spaced time index `day`
  # since trading days are not evenly distributed.
  mutate(day = row_number()) %>%
  update_tsibble(index = day, regular = TRUE)

google_2015 <- google_stock %>% filter(year(Date) == 2015) %>%
                  select(Symbol, Date, day, Close)

head(google_2015)

hilo() function to compute confidence intervals

Using the function hilo() prediction intervals are automatically computed by the fable library. Without any arguments, it computes the 80% and 95% confidence intervals

horiz = 5

google_stock <- gafa_stock %>%
  filter(Symbol == "GOOG", year(Date) >= 2015) %>%
  mutate(day = row_number()) %>%
  update_tsibble(index = day, regular = TRUE)

google_2015 <- google_stock %>% filter(year(Date) == 2015)

fit <- google_2015 %>%
        model(NAIVE(Close))

fc <- fit %>%
        forecast(h = horiz)

fc_hilo <- fc %>% hilo()
fc_hilo
# A tsibble: 5 x 7 [1]
# Key:       Symbol, .model [1]
  Symbol .model         day
  <chr>  <chr>        <dbl>
1 GOOG   NAIVE(Close)   253
2 GOOG   NAIVE(Close)   254
3 GOOG   NAIVE(Close)   255
4 GOOG   NAIVE(Close)   256
5 GOOG   NAIVE(Close)   257
# ℹ 4 more variables: Close <dist>, .mean <dbl>, `80%` <hilo>, `95%` <hilo>

Inspecting the confidence intervals

To extract the limits of the confidence intervals computed using hilo() we have a couple alternatives:

  1. (Not recommended) extract the particular element of the vector of confidence intervals:
# Vector of 80% conf intervals
pints_80 <- fc_hilo %>% pull(`80%`)
pints_80[1]
<hilo[1]>
[1] [744.54, 773.22]80

Then we can access the components lower, upper and level using the $ operator:

pints_80[1]$lower # Lower bound of the confidence interval
[1] 744.54
pints_80[1]$upper # Upper bound of the confidence interval
[1] 773.22
pints_80[1]$level # Confidence level
[1] 80
  1. Use the function unpack_hilo() to create new columns with the limits of the confidence intervals. In this case new columns *_lower and *_upper will be created to detail the limits of the confidence intervals we are unpacking. Remember that the column .mean() in the forecasts table is the mean of our forecast distribution, that is,
fc_hilo <- fc_hilo %>% 
  unpack_hilo(c(`80%`, `95%`))

fc_hilo %>%
  select(day, .mean, `80%_upper`, `80%_lower`, `95%_lower`, `95%_upper`)
# A tsibble: 5 x 6 [1]
    day .mean `80%_upper` `80%_lower` `95%_lower` `95%_upper`
  <dbl> <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>       <dbl>
1   253  759.        773.        745.        737.        781.
2   254  759.        779.        739.        728.        790.
3   255  759.        784.        734.        721.        797.
4   256  759.        788.        730.        715.        803.
5   257  759.        791.        727.        710.        808.

Check: mean of the forecast distribution (point forecast) is the center of the confidence interval

Importantly, if the forecast distribution is symmetric, the mean and the median will coincide. And remember that the point forecast is computed as the mean of the forecast distribution (column .mean of the fable):

# Compute midpoints of confidence intervals
midpoints <- fc_hilo %>%
  mutate(midpoints = (`95%_lower` + `95%_upper`)*0.5) %>% # Compute the midpoints of the 95% conf intervals
  pull(midpoints)

# Check that the column .mean is the midpoint of the confidence intervals
all.equal(midpoints, fc_hilo$`.mean`)
[1] TRUE

Plotting confidence intervals

When plotting the forecasts, the fable package prints prediction intervals by default unless the argument level is set to FALSE.

fc %>%
  autoplot(google_2015) +
  labs(title="Google daily closing stock price", y="$US" )

Again, let us now zoom in to focus solely on the region we forecasted. The figure below depicts the point forecast (blue line), the 80% and 95% confidence intervals (shaded blue regions) and the forecast distributions underneath. We can see that the model generates normal forecast distributions

Extracting parameters from forecast distributions

By now you should have noticed that, when generating forecasts, there is a column of type <S3 Distribution>. This column contains the information about the forecast distributions at each forecast horizon. The column always has the name of the response variable (the y variable) of the time series, in this case Close

fc %>% select(day, Close)
# A fable: 5 x 2 [1]
    day       Close
  <dbl>      <dist>
1   253 N(759, 125)
2   254 N(759, 250)
3   255 N(759, 376)
4   256 N(759, 501)
5   257 N(759, 626)

We can compute the parameters of our distribution using the function parameters within the package distributional. You may need to install that package. Here, in order to avoid loading the package, we will make an explicit reference to the package when calling the function (you may still need to install it though).

fc %>% pull(Close) %>% distributional::parameters()
      mu    sigma
1 758.88 11.18958
2 758.88 15.82446
3 758.88 19.38093
4 758.88 22.37917
5 758.88 25.02067

Check: manual computation of confidence intervals vs hilo() computation

Let us, as an example, compute manually the 95% prediction interval for the 1-step forecast of the example above (the google stock prices of 2015).

We noted before that, for a 1-step ahead confidence interval, the std. deviation of the forecast distribution can be estimated from the std. deviation of the residuals:

\[ \hat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{T-K}\sum_{t=1}^T e_t^2} \]

  • \(T\) is the length of the residuals (after removing NAs).
  • \(K\) is the number of parameters of the particular model being fitted

Using the formula above:

# Extract the residuals
res <- fit %>% augment() %>% pull(.innov)
# Remove missing values before computing the length
res <- res[!is.na(res)]

# Compute T and K
T = length(res) # T number of points in the residuals
K = nrow(tidy(fit)) # K number of parameters in our model. 0 for NAIVE model.

sigma_res = sqrt(sum(res^2, na.rm=TRUE)/(T-K))

# Check whether our result matches the std. deviation of the forecast distribution
sigma_res
[1] 11.18958
# Check that the standard deviation matches the fable computation
all.equal(sigma_res, distributional::parameters(fc$Close[1])$sigma)
[1] TRUE

With this information we can compute the confidence interval based on the point forecast (in this case the mean of the forecast distribution) and applying the formula:

\[ \hat{y}_{T+h|T} \pm c \hat\sigma_h, \]

where:

  • \(\hat\sigma_h\) is an estimate of the standard deviation of the \(h\)-step forecast distribution.
  • the multiplier \(c\) depends on the coverage probability and is equal to the corresponding quantile of the normal distribution. Usually we will compute 80% and 95% intervals, although another coverage may be used.

If we want a 95% confidence interval, that means we need the quantile corresponding to \(1-0.05/2 = 97.5%\) of the normal distribution (see table at the beginning of this notebook)

# Point forecaset, which in this case is the mean of the forecast distribution
y_hat <- fc$.mean[1]

# Quantile of the normal distribution
alpha = 0.05 # 95% confidence interval
quant = qnorm(1-alpha*0.5, 0, 1)

# Confidence interval computed manually
CI <- c(y_hat - quant*sigma_res, y_hat + quant*sigma_res)

# Confidence interval computed by fable library
CI_hilo <- c(fc_hilo$`95%_lower`[1], fc_hilo$`95%_upper`[1])

# Check of the value of the CI and that both CIs match
CI
[1] 736.9488 780.8112
# Check that the manually compted confidence intervals
# match with those returned by fable.
all.equal(CI, CI_hilo)
[1] TRUE

To compute intervals beyond a horizon of 1, we need to have the value of the estimation of the std. deviation of the forecast distribution for the particular forecast horizon. As we noted previously in this notebook, explicit formulas exist for the benchmark methods (Mean, Naive, SNaive and Drift). For more complex methods there is not such a general solution, but computational approaches tailored for every method exist. As long as the residuals fulfil uncorrelated, normality and homoskedasticity assumptions, the returned intervals are reasonable.

Prediction intervals can also be computed from bootstrapped residuals as we also noted earlier in the notebook. This assumes uncorrelated and homoskedastic residuals, but makes no assumption regarding normality.

Forecasting and transformations

When performing a transformation on the data:

  1. We produce forecasts of the transformed data, on the transformed domain.
  2. To obtain forecasts on the original domain, we need to back-transform to obtain forecasts on the original scale.

The box-cox transformation admits an explicit inverse, so this could also be performed manually. But the fable() package and any other good forecasting software will do this for you:

\[ \text{back-transform of box-cox: } \ \ \ \ y_{t} = \begin{cases} \exp(w_{t}) & \text{if $\lambda=0$};\\ \text{sign}(\lambda w_t+1)|\lambda w_t+1|^{1/\lambda} & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \]

The fable package performs this back-transformations automatically if the transformation has been used in the model definition.

Prediction intervals and tranformations

The forecast distribution is also transformed when reversing the transformation. Let us consider the figure below to discuss the transformation process:

When performing the transformation we want to stabilize the variance of the data, which will hopefully result in symmetrically distributed errors as in the distribution on the right of the image (transformed domain).

The forecsat distribution is assumed to inherit this symmetry. This, in the transformed domain (\(w_t\)) the forecast distribution will be symmetric, just as the error distribution. However, when returning to the original scale to provide the forecasts of \(y_t\), that distribution will not be symmetric. If the transformation is continuous and strictly monotonic (as is the Box-Cox transformation), then the quantiles will be preserved under this transformation as will the probability coverage of any interval in the transformed domain when back-transformed to the original domain.

  • The end points of the prediction intervals in the transformed domain are back-transformed to give a prediction interval on the original scale. This preserves the probability coverage of the prediction interval, but the prediction interval will no longer be symmetric around the point forecast. Or in other words, the back-transformed forecast will in general not be the mean of the forecast distribution.

  • If the forecast distribution in the transformed space is symmetric: the back transformed forecast will be the median of the forecast distribution in the original domain (original variables).

  • The difference between the back-transformed forecast and the mean is called the bias. When using the mean rather than the median, we say the point forecasts have been bias-adjusted.

    • Using the median may be acceptable in many forecasting sitations.
    • Some situations may require properties of the mean that are not shared with the median. In these situations you may require to recover the mean.
      • For example, adding sales forecasts for various regions requires using the mean of the forecast distribution and not the median, because medians do not add up
      • For example, forecasting a number of related products and you need the point forecasts to sum in order to give the forecast of total number of products.
    • The larger the forecast variance, the bigger the difference between the mean and the median. This can be concluded from the formulas below, which give an approximation the back-transformed mean in the original scale. In the formulas below \(\hat{w}_{T+h|T}\) is the \(h\)-step forecast mean and \(\sigma_h^2\) is the \(h\)-step forecast varianced on the transformed domain:

\[ \hat{y}_{T+h|T} = \begin{cases} \exp(\hat{w}_{T+h|T})\left[1 + \frac{\sigma_h^2}{2}\right] & \text{if $\lambda=0$;}\\ (\lambda \hat{w}_{T+h|T}+1)^{1/\lambda}\left[1 + \frac{\sigma_h^2(1-\lambda)}{2(\lambda \hat{w}_{T+h|T}+1)^{2}}\right] & \text{otherwise;} \end{cases} \]

The back-transformations computed automatically by fable achieve the following`:

  1. Forecast are returned in the original domain rather than in the transformed domain (provided that the transformation has been properly specified upon model definition).
  2. Forecast medians are automatically converted into forecast means (bias-adjusted).

The following example illustrates three important points:

  1. How the log transformation is applied upon defining the model rather than before so that the fable package is able to perform the back transformation automatically. That is, so that the package knows there is a transformation involved.
  2. The code to tell the fable package to depict both the mean and median point forecasts of the back transformed forecast distributions.
  3. Most importantly: you can see that the back transformed forecast distribution is not symmetric. The mean does not coincide with the median and neither the mean nor the median coincide with the midpoint of the domain of the forecast distribution.
# Create a new column to hold the transformed variable
prices <- prices %>%
  mutate(log_eggs = log(eggs))
# forecast horizon
horiz = 50

# Model 1: fitted to the variable already transformed
fit1 <- prices %>%
  filter(!is.na(eggs)) %>%
  model(drift = RW(log_eggs ~ drift()))

# fc1: forecasts generated with model 1
fc1 <- fit1 %>%
  forecast(h = horiz)

# Model 2: fitted to the original variable specifying the transformation upon model definition
fit2 <- prices %>%
  filter(!is.na(eggs)) %>% # This line simply selects values that are not NAs from the time series
  model(RW(log(eggs) ~ drift()))
 
# fc2: forecasts generated with model 2
fc2 <- fit2 %>%
  forecast(h = horiz)

# figures for each model
fig1 <- fc1 %>%
  autoplot(prices %>% filter(!is.na(eggs)),
           level = 80, point_forecast = lst(mean, median) # Depict both mean and median in the back transformed forecasts
           ) +
  labs(title = "log(Annual egg prices)",
       y = "log($US cents infl. adj)") +
  theme(legend.position="none") # Remove legend for mean and median to have more space for the plots

fig2 <- fc2 %>%
  autoplot(prices %>% filter(!is.na(eggs)),
           level = 80, point_forecast = lst(mean, median) # Depict both mean and median in the back transformed forecasts
           ) +
  labs(title = "Annual egg prices",
       y = "$US cents infl. adj") +
  theme(legend.position="none") # Remove legend for mean and median to have more space for the plots

fig1 + fig2

In the above graph:

  • The right side depicts the series and the forecasts in the original domain, once everything has been back-transformed. The mean of the forecast distribution is represented by the continuous blue line, will the median is represented by the dashed line. The further ahead into the future, the greater the divergence between these two values. It is clear that these forecast distributions are not symmetric.
  • The left side represents the series and the forecasts in the transformed domain. We can see that the mean coincides with the median, i.e., the forecast distribution in the transformed domain is symmetric. It is when back-transforming that this symmetry is lost.

The figure below focuses only on the forecasting region and shows the forecast distributions on the transformed domain (left) and on the original domain (right), to further emphasize this loss of symmetry when back-transforming.

  • Remember that the coverage of the prediction intervals computed in the transformed domain is preserved when back-transforming as long as the transformation is strictly monotonic (as is the case). The difference now is that, in the original domain, these prediction intervals are not symmetric around the mean of the forecast distribution as they are in the transformed domain.

Understanding forecasts returned when using transformations

Remember that, in the previous example, we have fitted two models:

  • Model 1: fitted to the transformed variable log_eggs = log(eggs)
# Model 1: fitted to the variable already transformed
fit1 <- prices %>%
  filter(!is.na(eggs)) %>%
  model(drift = RW(log_eggs ~ drift()))
  • Model 2: fitted to the original variable, detailing the transformation upon model definition:
# Model 2: fitted to the original variable specifying the transformation upon model definition
fit2 <- prices %>%
  filter(!is.na(eggs)) %>% # This line simply selects values that are not NAs from the time series
  model(RW(log(eggs) ~ drift()))

See the code snippets above for further details. With those models we generated two forecast objects:

  • fc1, generated using model 1. Therefore it returns forecasts in the transformed domain (it is working with the transformed variable directly).
head(fc1, 4)
# A fable: 4 x 4 [1Y]
# Key:     .model [1]
  .model  year      log_eggs
  <chr>  <dbl>        <dist>
1 drift   1994 N(4.1, 0.018)
2 drift   1995 N(4.1, 0.036)
3 drift   1996 N(4.1, 0.055)
4 drift   1997 N(4.1, 0.074)
# ℹ 1 more variable: .mean <dbl>
  • fc2 generated using model 2. fable knows we have applied a transformation in model2 and is therefore capable of back-transforming to the original domain. It does so and returns forecasts that are bias-adjusted, i.e., it returns the mean of the back-transformed forecast distribution (column .mean)
head(fc2, 4)
# A fable: 4 x 4 [1Y]
# Key:     .model [1]
  .model                   year             eggs .mean
  <chr>                   <dbl>           <dist> <dbl>
1 RW(log(eggs) ~ drift())  1994 t(N(4.1, 0.018))  61.8
2 RW(log(eggs) ~ drift())  1995 t(N(4.1, 0.036))  61.4
3 RW(log(eggs) ~ drift())  1996 t(N(4.1, 0.055))  61.0
4 RW(log(eggs) ~ drift())  1997 t(N(4.1, 0.074))  60.6

Performing some checks on the forecasts and forecast distributions

Check 1: back-transforming the bounds of the prediction intervals in the transformed domain to obtain the prediction intervals in the original domain.
# Comopute lower and upper bounds of 80% and 95% confidence intervals
# in the transformed domain
fc1_intervals <- 
  fc1 %>% 
    hilo() %>% 
    unpack_hilo(c(`80%`, `95%`)) 

# Comopute lower and upper bounds of 80% and 95% confidence intervals
# in the original domain
fc2_intervals <- 
  fc2 %>% 
    hilo() %>% 
    unpack_hilo(c(`80%`, `95%`))

# Backtransform 95% lowerbound
fc2_95lower_manual <- exp(fc1_intervals$`95%_lower`)
fc2_95lower_fable <- fc2_intervals$`95%_lower`

# Backtransform 95% upperbound
fc2_95upper_manual <- exp(fc1_intervals$`95%_upper`)
fc2_95upper_fable <- fc2_intervals$`95%_upper`

# CHECK
all.equal(fc2_95lower_manual, fc2_95lower_fable)
[1] TRUE
all.equal(fc2_95upper_manual, fc2_95upper_fable)
[1] TRUE
Check 2: Mean of prediction intervals in transformed domain back-transforms to median in the original domain
# Back-transform forecasts in the transformed domain (back-transform mean)
fc1_backtransf <- exp(fc1$.mean)

# Compute medians of distributions of fc2
# fc2$eggs is a vector containing the forecast distributions of fc2
fc2_median <- median(fc2$eggs)

# CHECK
all.equal(fc1_backtransf, fc2_median)
[1] TRUE
Check 3: Forecasts in the original domain are automatically biased-adjusted by the library fable, returning the mean of the back-transformed confidence intervals
# Compute medians of distributions of fc2
fc2_mean_manual <- mean(fc2$eggs)

# Point forecasts (bias-adjusted)
fc2_point <- fc2$.mean

# CHECK
all.equal(fc2_mean_manual, fc2_point)
[1] TRUE

As we can see above, the fable() package is automatically returning bias adjusted forecasts (forecasts on the mean). If we want to preserve the forecast on the median, we can compute them by computing the median of the forecast distributions. The following returns the median of all the forecast distributions (the median for every forecast horizon).

  • NOTE: remember that the column eggs of the object fc2 holds the distribution objects.
median(fc2$eggs)

Exercise 1

Use decomposition_model() in combination with an STL decomposition and a log transformation to generate a 36 step-forecast of the retail_series used in exercise 1 of notebook 6_1. Back transform the result to the original variables depicting both the mean and median point forecasts.

As in notebook 6_1, use a drift model to fit the seasonally adjusted data and a seasonal naive model to fit the seasonal component.

retail_series <- aus_retail %>%
  filter(`Series ID` == "A3349767W")
